definition: Intrepid means fearless and brave in the face of danger.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word intrepid. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know intrepid should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Intrepid to the last, the retired smokejumper asked only which ridge needed her.
Bold takes confident risks in daily life and stops short of intrepid, which keeps its nerve in genuine danger.
Foolhardy goes further than intrepid — past courage entirely, into ignoring danger that ought to be respected.

Fearless is the flat statement that no fear is present at all -- nothing in the word says the danger was real or the trial hard. Intrepid tells a richer story: genuine danger, fear likely felt, and nerve held steady anyway. You can be fearless of spiders; expeditions call for intrepid.

Dauntless means impossible to discourage -- however long the ordeal grinds on, the resolve never breaks. It measures persistence against setbacks. Intrepid measures the moment of danger itself: steady nerve while the stakes are genuine. A dauntless campaigner outlasts years; an intrepid rescuer holds firm tonight.

Daring is drawn to risk for its flair -- the showman's cousin, happiest with an audience: a daring dress, a daring menu. Intrepid has no interest in show; it is steady nerve under genuine danger. Daring courts the gasp; intrepid simply does the dangerous thing well.

When the kayaker capsized beyond the breakers, the seventeen-year-old lifeguard swam out through a squall that had emptied the beach — not recklessly, but with the trained, steady nerve the word intrepid was made for.
Intrepid is literally 'not trembling' — in- ('not') + trepidus ('alarmed') — and it needs real danger to earn it.
Bold risks embarrassment; daring loves flair; intrepid keeps its nerve where the stakes are genuine.
Intrepid carries a whiff of the expedition poster — reserve it for genuine danger met with steady nerve.
Daring celebrates flair and risk-taking (a daring menu, a daring dress); bold is confidence anywhere; brave is the plain, warm word.
Calling the office coffee run intrepid is a joke, and works as one.

Mara Voss photographs flooded caves, and she will tell anyone that the job frightens her every single time.
Before the Cenote Azul dive she sat on the tailgate for ten minutes, breathing slowly, listing aloud everything that could go wrong.
Then she checked her lines twice, entered the water, and worked calmly for an hour in a passage no wider than her shoulders.
Her editor calls her intrepid, and is careful about the word: not the absence of dread, but the discipline to work steadily through it while the danger is real.
The one diver Mara refuses to partner with is the one who claims to feel nothing down there.
